title: The black stone
hookLine: pilgrims kiss, touch or point to it, as the Prophet ﷺ did

lines: I KNOW YOU ARE A STONE.
cards: Umar ibn al-Khattab walks up to a corner of the Ka'ba, bends toward a dark stone set into the wall, and kisses it. Then he straightens up and speaks to it. The words are kept in Sahih al-Bukhari, and they're blunt.
I know you are a stone. You can neither harm nor help. If I had not seen the Prophet kiss you, I would not have kissed you.
Today, the stone, and why a man who said all that still bent down to it.

teach.h: THE CORNER WHERE EACH CIRCUIT BEGINS.
teach.b: First, where it is. The black stone is set into one corner of the Ka'ba, the corner where each circuit of yesterday's tawaf begins and ends. Second, Umar's words, and what they guard against.
He says out loud what someone watching might wonder: is this stone a power? No.

teach.h: IT CAN NEITHER HARM NOR HELP.
teach.b: It can't harm and it can't help. Whatever honor it has comes from one place: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ honored it. So the kiss isn't worship of a stone.
It's following a person, in a small physical way, exactly as he did. Third, the crowds. Today, getting close enough to kiss the stone can mean a long, hard push through a packed crowd.

Here another report in Bukhari helps. Ibn Abbas says the Prophet once went around the House riding a camel, and whenever he came to the corner, he pointed to it and said Allahu akbar. He didn't get down.
So pilgrims have three ways: kiss it if you can reach it, touch it with a hand, or, from a distance, raise a hand toward it and say God is greatest. Fourth, what that means for the crowd.
In this report, the pointing isn't a fallback. It's the Prophet's own way that day. Nobody needs to shove an old man aside to honor a stone that, in Umar's words, can't help anyone.

teach.h: THE RAISED HAND IS A FULL GREETING.
teach.b: A raised hand from far back in the crowd is a full greeting. A salute to the corner, and the circuit goes on.

how: During tawaf, pilgrims begin each circuit at the black stone; those who can reach it kiss or touch it, and others raise a hand toward it from a distance and say Allahu akbar.

o: a sacred rock believed to heal and protect whoever touches it
a stone in the Ka'ba's corner, kissed, touched or saluted
the dark cloth that covers the Ka'ba all year round

games.q: the black stone — tap the pairs.
p: I know you are a stone

s: in Umar's words, the black stone has power to help
Umar said it can neither harm nor help; he kissed it only because the Prophet did.
pointing to the stone from a distance is the Prophet's own practice
Ibn Abbas reports he pointed to the corner from his camel, in Bukhari.
a pilgrim must kiss the stone or the tawaf doesn't count
pilgrims kiss it, touch it, or point to it from a distance.

games.q: you're Umar, standing at the black stone. people are watching. what do you do?
o: kiss it, then say aloud it's only a stone, kissed because the Prophet kissed it.
games.why: he kisses it, then tells it: it can neither harm nor help, and he'd not have kissed it had he not seen the Prophet do so.

practice: Find which way Mecca lies from where you are, the qiblah, with a phone compass or a prayer app, and turn to face it. Slowly raise your right hand toward it, the way a pilgrim does from far back in the crowd.
If you pray, say Allahu akbar quietly; if not, hold the gesture for a breath and notice the distance it crosses.

wordCard.voice: The black stone. The stone in the corner of the Ka'ba that pilgrims kiss, touch, or point to, as the Prophet did. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a salute to the corner. A small gesture from far away still reaches. See you at the station.
